name: Daria Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the repairs team for Northgate Homes, the housing association that owns most of the flats on our side of town. A normal day, I pick up the van at half seven and I've got six or seven jobs on the tablet: a dead storage heater, a shower that trips the board, a light fitting full of water from the flat upstairs. I like that I'm fixing things for people who've usually been waiting too long. What wears me out is the damp, honestly, and walking into the same mouldy flats month after month knowing the real fix is a roof nobody will pay for.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how are things for you at home, money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a two-bed with my friend Priya, who works at the pharmacy on the high street. My pay's on the low side for an electrician, and I send my mum a bit each month since her hours got cut at the school kitchen. So savings are basically a few weeks of rent. There's not much else round here for sparks either, it's Northgate or a long commute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. So, roughly the world we've got now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, maybe now the money goes into fixing roofs instead of chatbots. At work there's been a lot of talk about AI handling tenant calls, and plenty of us thought it'd be a mess. Online I'd probably share something about putting public money into homes, not tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's pretty safe in that world. Northgate isn't going anywhere and the flats keep breaking. What keeps me up is that I'm one boiler, or one month of my mum needing more, away from a credit card I can't clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the job and keep using the AI on the tablet for writing up job notes, because it does save me ten minutes a day. I'd ask about the overtime rota for emergency call-outs, because that's an extra hundred or so a weekend. And I'd talk to Gwen, our union rep, about the pay review coming up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, with a low hum of money worry. It's the same hum I've had since my apprenticeship. Nothing about this picture makes it louder, but nothing makes it go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI on the tablet. When did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a year ago, once a couple of the older lads swore by it. You say what you found and it writes the job note properly, with the right codes. I was sceptical, but it's good for that, and I'm not about to pretend otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra call-out money go towards first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a cushion. I'd like one full month of rent sitting there, untouched, so that when Mum rings I don't have to think twice. Right now it's about two-thirds of a month on a good week.

say: I'd say the money should go into **fixing roofs**, not chatbots.
I'd share posts online about putting **public money** into homes instead of tech.
think: My job at the **housing association** feels safe because the flats keep breaking.
The real worry is being **one boiler** or one family crisis away from unpayable debt.
do: Keep using the **tablet AI** for job notes, which saves ten minutes a day.
Sign up for the **call-out rota** for about a hundred extra a weekend.
Talk to the **union rep** about the coming pay review.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with a low hum of money worry that predates AI.
S0.quote: I'm one boiler, or one month of my mum needing more, away from a credit card I can't clear.
fieldNote: Her job feels **secure**, but helping her mother keeps her cushion paper-thin.
She adopted AI **once proven** by older colleagues, and is honest that it helps.
Her first goal is **one month of rent** saved, a modest and concrete target.
Her politics point blame at **underfunded housing**, not at tenants or coworkers.

steps.text: Keep writing job notes with the tablet's AI helper
Join the weekend emergency call-out rota for extra pay
Raise the pay review with Gwen, the union rep

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking and answering customers. That's our whole repairs call centre, basically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to protect the call centre staff, because those are our mates in the office. I'd say it at the union meeting too. Online I'd say the savings should go into more repair teams, not shareholder bonuses, though we don't have shareholders, so maybe into the chief exec's car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job changes but probably doesn't go. The software would plan my route and book my slots, and I'd bet the targets go from seven jobs a day to nine. That's not losing my job, but it's losing the bit of slack that lets me have a cuppa with an old fella on his own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new scheduling system properly once it's rolled out, not before. I'd push through the union for a cap on daily jobs, so the software can't just pile them on. And I'd look into the heat pump installer course, because the association keeps talking about retrofits and that's work the software creates, not takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit sad. I'm fine, I think. But the people on the phones in the office, some of them have been there twenty years, and they're the ones who'll go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra on the repairs line. She knows every tenant by voice, she knows who's poorly and who's just lonely. A system that books jobs can't tell a carer that a tenant hasn't answered the phone in three days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the heat pump course rather than learning more AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can see the work coming. Northgate has hundreds of flats on old electric heating, and if they get grants to swap them, someone has to wire it. I'll use whatever app they give me, but the skill I want is the one in my hands.

say: I'd stand up at the union meeting to **protect call-centre staff**, our mates in the office.
I'd argue the savings should fund **more repair teams**, not executive perks.
think: My job changes rather than goes, with software **planning my route** and booking slots.
Targets would rise from **seven to nine** jobs a day, killing the slack for lonely tenants.
do: Learn the **scheduling system** properly once it's rolled out, not before.
Push through the union for a **cap on daily jobs**.
Look into the **heat pump installer** course for coming retrofits.
feel: **Uneasy** about tighter targets, though her own job seems safe.
**Sad** for long-serving office staff who will likely lose their jobs.
S1.quote: A system that books jobs can't tell a carer that a tenant hasn't answered the phone in three days.
fieldNote: She sees the hit landing on **office colleagues** first, and worries more for them.
Her fear is **rising targets**, which would squeeze the human side of her work.
She'd retrain towards **retrofit work** that the change creates rather than resist it.
A steady adopter: she'll learn the system **once it's live**, not ahead of time.

steps.text: Learn the new scheduling system once Northgate rolls it out
Push the union for a cap on daily repair jobs
Sign up for the heat pump installer course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Gosh. And then robots in five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this needs a government plan, now, not a review in three years. At work I'd be pushing the union to get a no-redundancy deal before anyone at the top decides anything. Online I'd be sharing every campaign for public housing and a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the robots are what get me, not the AGI. The thinking side of my job, the notes and codes and ordering parts, goes in 2028, fine. But by 2031 Northgate will be broke from tenants losing their jobs, and a robot that does storage heaters for half my wage is exactly what a broke landlord buys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the heat pump course straight away, this winter, even if I have to put it on a card. I'd get Priya and me to look at whether we could move to a smaller, cheaper flat. And I'd stop sending Mum money, which I'd hate, but I can't help her if I'm sinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Proper scared, the stomach kind. Two years isn't long enough for anyone to get their act together, and I'd be thirty-two when the robots come, with nothing behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop sending your mum money. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. I'd go round on a Sunday and tell her straight, and she'd say she understands, and then she'd skip meals and not tell me. That's the bit I keep picturing, her pretending she's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do the course on a credit card when you're worried about debt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in this one, waiting is worse. If I'm not one of the people who can install the new heating before the robots come, I'm nothing to them. It's a gamble, but standing still is a bigger one.

say: I'd demand a **government plan now**, not a review in three years.
I'd push the union for a **no-redundancy deal** before management decides anything.
think: **Robots by 2031** worry me more than AGI, because broke landlords buy cheap labour.
Tenants losing jobs would leave the association **short of rent money**.
do: Start the **heat pump course** this winter, even if it goes on a card.
Look with her flatmate at moving to a **cheaper flat**.
Stop **sending money** to her mother to stay afloat.
feel: **Exposed**, facing robots at thirty-two with nothing saved behind her.
S2.quote: A robot that does storage heaters for half my wage is exactly what a broke landlord buys.
fieldNote: She tracks the **chain reaction**: tenants lose jobs, rent falls, robots get bought.
She'd take on **card debt** to retrain, judging standing still as the bigger risk.
Cutting help to her **mother** is the decision that pains her most.
Her politics turn **urgent**: basic income, public housing and union deals.

steps.text: Start the heat pump installer course this winter on a card
Stop the monthly money she sends her mum
Look with Priya for a smaller, cheaper flat
Push the union for a no-redundancy deal at Northgate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years to AGI, eight to the robots. That's more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a huge deal, but this time we've got time to do it properly. At work I'd tell people to get their tickets now, the heat pump, the solar, the battery stuff. Online I'd say this is the moment to fund the trades colleges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right for longer than most. By 2034 I'd be thirty-five with maybe ten years of retrofit work behind me. But all those years I'm earning, I'm also watching the people I fix things for lose everything, and that's going to wear on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the heat pump course next year, properly saved for this time, maybe through the union learning fund. I'd try the AI design tools for heating layouts once a few people I trust have used them. And I'd finally build that one month of rent, then two, before anything big lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but more in a planning way. Five years feels like long enough to get my feet under me. It doesn't feel long enough for the world around me, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change for your tenants in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot of them already work in shops and warehouses, and call centres. If those jobs go in 2031, they're in rent arrears by 2032. I'd be wiring new heating into flats where people can't afford to switch it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try the AI design tools. What would make you trust them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing Gwen's brother use one. He does heating design for a bigger firm, and if he says it gets the sizing right, I'll try it. I don't need to be first, I just don't want to be last.

say: I'd tell coworkers to get their **retrofit tickets** now: heat pump, solar and battery.
I'd say online this is the moment to **fund trades colleges**.
think: I'd likely have **ten years** of retrofit work before robots arrive at thirty-five.
Watching tenants **lose everything** while I keep earning would wear on me.
do: Take the **heat pump course** next year, funded by savings or the union.
Try **AI design tools** once trusted people have used them.
Build up **one month's rent**, then two, before anything big lands.
feel: **Worried**, but in a planning way rather than a frightened one.
**Uneasy** that five years is enough for her but not for her tenants.
S3.quote: I'd be wiring new heating into flats where people can't afford to switch it on.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **plan the retrofit route** instead of gambling on debt.
Her worry shifts toward **tenants' arrears**, which could still sink her employer.
She sets a clear trust test: try tools once **a trusted user** vouches.
Still anxious because robots arrive around **thirty-five** with a thin cushion.

steps.text: Take the heat pump course next year through the union fund
Try AI heating-design tools after a trusted user vouches
Save one month's rent, then two, in a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best of the bad versions, because there's time to change the rules. I'd be on at the union to get robot-safety sign-off written into contracts. Online I'd say ten years is enough to retrain a whole town, if anyone bothers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough for me to become the person who manages the retrofit crews, or checks the robots' work. I'd be forty-ish when robots come. The question is whether Northgate still has money then, or whether the whole town's broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the heat pump ticket over the next couple of years, then the inspection one. I'd look at the supervisor role that comes up every few years, and actually go for it. And I'd keep sending Mum her bit, because with ten years I can carry her and still build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. There's still the money hum, and still the question of what the town looks like. But I can breathe in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from Northgate to stay there for ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training on their time, not mine, and a proper path up. I've seen people go for supervisor and get told to wait another year, for five years. If Northgate wants me to stay through all this, they need to show me the ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if they didn't, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at the council's own repairs team or a bigger contractor in the city, even with the commute. I don't want to leave, my mum's here and Priya's here. But I'd go if the ladder only exists on paper.

say: I'd call it the **best of the bad** versions, because rules can still change.
I'd push the union to write **robot-safety sign-off** into contracts.
think: Ten years is enough to become a **crew manager** or the person checking robots' work.
The real question is whether the **housing association** still has money by then.
do: Get the **heat pump ticket**, then the inspection ticket, over a few years.
Apply for the **supervisor role** next time it comes up.
Keep **supporting her mother** while still building savings.
feel: **Calmer** but not calm, with the old money hum still there.
Able to **breathe**, though unsure what the town will look like.
S4.quote: If Northgate wants me to stay through all this, they need to show me the ladder.
fieldNote: A decade lets her keep **helping her mother**, which mattered to her a lot.
She wants a **real promotion path** and would leave if it only exists on paper.
Still anxious because her employer's **money** depends on tenants' jobs.
Moving away is a **last resort** because her mother and flatmate are local.

steps.text: Get the heat pump ticket, then the inspection ticket
Apply for the repairs supervisor role when it opens
Apply to the council repairs team if no promotion comes

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time for anyone, not me, not Northgate, not the tenants. What would actually help is paid retraining for trades before it hits, and someone guaranteeing rent support for people in social housing, because if they go under, so do we.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who we're each carrying. I'm twenty-seven with no kids, but I've got my mum. Lots of people my age are quietly holding up a parent, and that changes every choice.

headlineQuote: Lots of people my age are quietly holding up a parent, and that changes every choice.
portrait: Daria is a **27-year-old electrician** on a housing association's repairs team, fixing heaters and leaks in social flats.
She shares a flat with a friend and **sends money** to her mother, so her savings stay thin.
She uses **AI for job notes** after older colleagues proved it, and adopts tools once others trust them.
Her answer to change is **retrofit work**: heat pumps and inspection tickets, backed by union deals.
She moves from **uneasy to alarmed**, worrying most about tenants' jobs and her employer's money.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because nobody, from her to her employer to the tenants, would have time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** for tradespeople before the change hits.
Guaranteed **rent support** for social housing tenants, since her job depends on them.
